newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo, Germany sign investment protection agreement.
newsitem.headline: Yugo, Germany sign investment protection agreement.

text.p: Yugoslavia and Germany signed an agreement on the protection of mutual investments, paving the way to renewing economic ties after four and a half years of sanctions.

"Our joint task now is balancing trade, since in the first eight months this year our imports from Germany were nearly four times greater than exports to it," said Serbian Chamber of Commerce head Vlajko Stojiljkovic.
But the German deputy economy minister Hans Schilla warned Yugoslavia would have to make some major changes if it was to ever achieve that balance.

"Yugoslavia is competing with many countries for German investments, for example in Asia. There is readiness on our part, but much has to be done on the part of Yugoslavia with regard to reforms and overall liberalisation of the economy," Schilla said.

A 60-member delegation of Germany's top industrial and commercial companies arrived in Belgrade on Monday to discuss ways to boost cooperation following the lifting of the international trade embargo against Yugoslavia last Tuesday.
Germany ranks among Yugoslavia's top trading partners, with Yugoslav exports in the January-August period worth $78 million and imports $281 million.
There is a vast market in Yugoslavia for equipment, spare parts and other goods from Germany, but it would also like to sell its products, Stojiljkovic said.

"One of the reasons for the trade imbalance are obstacles that are still there for Yugoslav goods to enter the European Union markets, and we hope the German government will help in removing them," he said.
Stojiljkovic suggested German producers should be more oriented to cooperating with their Yugoslav counterparts, and not just selling their products on the local market.
But Schilla said Yugoslavia needed to do more on privatisation, restructuring of the banking sector and other reforms in order to bring the economic systems of the two countries closer.

"Our economy is market oriented and naturally cooperation is better with countries of the same orientation, where the state does not intervene, but where the market is dictated by economic subjects," he said, adding: "Confidence in the legal system is vital."
The German delegation includes representatives of giants like Siemens, Hoechst, Thyssen, Krupp, Boss-Telecomm, ABB, Mercedes-Benz and others. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom + 381 11 2224305
